newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean bankruptcy crisis exposes reform need.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean bankruptcy crisis exposes reform need.

text.p: The collapse of South Korea's Hanbo Steel Co in a loans scandal has exposed the need to eliminate corruption by speeding up financial restructuring, analysts said on Monday.
"The government will try to expedite financial restructuring to avoid another embarrassment like the Hanbo scandal," said Kim Byong-sok, an analyst at Hannuri-Salomon Securities.
Some analysts warned, however, that change could be delayed because President Kim Young-sam's administration may not favour drastic change in a presidential election year.
"Speedy reform could result in some painful adjustments which the government might not want to risk in a politically important year," said Im Joon-hwan, a banking analyst at Schroders Securities.
The nation's second largest steelmaker borrowed five trillion won ($5.8 billion), about 20 times its net worth, mainly to finance a new steel mill which analysts said made no economic sense.
Hanbo Steel, flagship of Hanbo Group -- the nation's 14th largest business -- was declared insolvent on January 23.
Opposition parties called the loans the biggest financial scandal in the nation's history and have accused the government of peddling influence to pressure banks into offering loans.

Last week, the Office of Bank Supervision blamed banks for extending loans to Hanbo Steel without proper credit analysis. The bank watchdog plans to announce disciplinary punishments on Tuesday against banks and their executives involved in the scandal.
Moody's Investors Service lowered the long-term ratings of the three Korean banks -- Korea Exchange Bank, Korea First Bank and Cho Hung Bank -- with the biggest exposure to Hanbo Steel.
The ratings agency said that its action reflected the continued deterioration in the banks' asset quality.
Analysts said the banking industry has been plagued by corruption, risky loans and poor credit screening.

A total of 18 heads of local banks have been placed in custody or forced to resign since President Kim took office in 1993 on an anti-corruption platform, they said. Most were found to have received bribes from borrowers.
Prosecutors have indicted 10 people over the Hanbo scandal, including three bankers -- two former presidents of Korea First Bank, Hanbo's biggest creditor, and the head of Cho Hung Bank.

"Punishment from the bank watchdog, downgrade in ratings and arrests of bankers would not put an end to the irregularities in the industry," said Im of Schroders. "It's a structural problem that can only be solved by reform."
Successive South Korean governments have used the country's banks as tools of their industrial policy, forcing them to extend loans which amounted to treating them as state cashiers.
Analysts said the introduction of private bank ownership would enable banks to be more responsible in giving out loans.
Currently, bank ownership is diluted with non-government shareholders limited to a maximum four percent holding. Bank heads are chosen by senior officials and approved by the bank watchdog.
"The owners would try to make a careful credit analysis in their investments and make as much profit as possible," said Kim of Hannuri-Salomon.
Mergers are widely seen as an inevitable consequence of a shake-up in the inefficient banking system.
"Mergers will help local banks prepare for market opening scheduled for the end of 1998," said Kim.
